A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching the retained Gaussian and denoising experiments across renumbering.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.2 and Appendix B report original Gaussian inference and image-denoising experiments, including quantitative results and sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: Sections 5.1–5.4 and Appendix B report original results for the retained benchmarks, Ricker-model hyperparameter exploration, and empirical human decision-making data.

M1.justification: The NPE-MMD and NPE-DANN procedures, objectives in Equations 3–7, and gradient-reversal mechanism remain unchanged. Task-specific network configurations and hyperparameter exploration extend evaluation without introducing a new proposed method component.

E1.justification: v2 adds contaminated Ricker population-dynamics inference and diffusion-model inference on empirical Implicit Association Test data. These introduce temporal ecological simulations and human response-time modeling beyond the retained Gaussian and MNIST/USPS denoising coverage.

E2.justification: The matched benchmarks retain the same comparison participants: NPE, NNPE, NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, and the analytic posterior for Gaussian inference. The new applications reuse the neural comparator set. NNPE standardization and noise scaling concern experimental settings.

E3.justification: Denoising evaluation changes from observed images seen during adaptation to a separate unseen test set. Gaussian test sets increase from 100 to 1,000, with posterior samples increasing from 100 to 5,000; denoising samples increase from 10 to 100. PPD changes to RMSE with denoised/resimulated references, and v2 adds NLL, C2ST diagnostics, and a 50-trial-per-method tuning protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic Ricker hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, t-SNE examinations of summary-space alignment, and real-data analyses of cleaning and prior–posterior convergence. Conversely, v1 Figures B6–B8, which directly measure approximation distances to the analytic posterior, are removed. The existing Gaussian domain and regularization analyses remain.

E5.justification: Gaussian reporting changes from averages over three runs to medians over ten runs, explicitly because extreme failures distort means. Ricker analyses introduce Gaussian-process trend estimates with 95% predictive intervals. Denoising retains its existing three-run mean and standard-deviation reporting.

E6.justification: New findings include Ricker calibration–error trade-offs and NNPE's advantage on misspecified human response times, where UDA provides no comparable benefit. Retained results also change: Table 1 reports likelihood-scale NPE-MMD NRMSE at lambda = 0.1 as 0.323 in v1 versus 0.189 in v2. These are replaced results under revised evaluation conditions, not a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2.2 extends the PPD definition with a denoised-reference variant, changing the reference quantity used in the distance. The main theoretical content—the UDA bound, typical-set definition, posterior targets, objectives, and Appendix A definition of amortization—remains unchanged. No new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central contributions and claims about likelihood versus prior misspecification remain. The claimed empirical scope expands to practical applications, while the conclusion replaces v1's two-step diagnostic recommendation with a more qualified assessment emphasizing unresolved obstacles to practical deployment.

C2.justification: v2 Section 6 explains that comparing predictions with noisy observations can penalize successful noise removal, qualifying v1's recommendation to diagnose robustness using SSDD followed by PPD. It adds substantive limitations concerning label-free hyperparameter selection, interpretability, and failure of majority-domain alignment to protect rare misspecified observations.

D1.justification: New appendices document Ricker architectures and search ranges, decision-model networks and training budgets, empirical-data selection, cleaning thresholds, and Mahalanobis-based test-set classification. NNPE standardization and image-noise scaling are explicitly documented. One reproducibility inconsistency remains: Gaussian adaptation data number 48,000 in Section 5.2 but 49,000 in Appendix B.4.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the cited context to ecological dynamics and cognitive decision modeling, including Ricker, Wood, Greenwald, Ratcliff, and Project Implicit literature. It also adds UDA validation, recent SBI misspecification, and Bayesian model-comparison connections. Positioning against Huang and Swierc remains largely unchanged; Huang's year correction does not identify a new work.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized around four studies and three families of metrics. Appendix metric explanations gain corresponding subsections, retained results passages are rewritten, and the short conclusion becomes an extended Discussion covering mechanisms, regularization, practical measurement, and future work.

P2.justification: v2 adds a method schematic, hyperparameter-response plots, t-SNE panels, and empirical-data figures, while removing the direct analytic-posterior distance panels. Existing plots and tables are relocated and recaptioned, including switching the introductory scatterplot scenario. Typography, author layout, headings, and page composition are also substantially reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial gaps in evidence for amortized generalization and practical robustness through unseen-image evaluation, larger posterior samples, systematic tuning analyses, and a real-data application exposing an important failure mode. Its discussion also qualifies the earlier diagnostic recommendation by recognizing the problem with noisy PPD references. These gains outweigh the loss of direct analytic-posterior distance plots, although omitted high-lambda results and inconsistent Gaussian budget reporting remain weaknesses.
